title: Exercise: images as arrays & geometric transforms
text:
By hand
B1. Sketch what the shear H = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2\\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} does to the unit square with corners (0,0), (1,0), (1,1), (0,1). What is \det H, and what does that say about the area?
B2. For each matrix, say whether the result is a mirror image, and give the factor by which areas change: (a) \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0\\ 0 & 0.5\end{bmatrix} (b) \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0\\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} (c) \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 0\\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix} (d) \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1\\ 0.5 & 0.5\end{bmatrix}
B3. The image is scaled by A = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 0\\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} about the origin. Which input position does the output pixel at \mathbf{x}' = (3, 5) come from?
B4. Bilinear interpolation. Four neighbouring pixels have the values I(0,0) = 10, I(1,0) = 20, I(0,1) = 30, I(1,1) = 60 (written as I(x, y)). Estimate I(0.25, 0.5): first interpolate along x on the rows y = 0 and y = 1, then along y. What does nearest-neighbour give?
B5. Rotate by 90° counter-clockwise about the point \mathbf{p} = (2, 1), without matrices: shift \mathbf{p} to the origin, turn a quarter turn, shift back. Where do the points (3, 1) and (2, 3) go? Check your answers with a sketch.
B6. Let S stretch the image by 2 along x (keep y), and R rotate it by 90° counter-clockwise about the centre. Where does the point (1, 0) go if you apply S first and then R? And if you apply R first and then S? A square image: is it tall or wide afterwards, in each case?






Solutions





B1. H keeps (1, 0) and sends (0, 1) to (2, 1): horizontal lines stay horizontal and every point slides sideways by twice its height. The square becomes a parallelogram with corners (0,0), (1,0), (3,1), (2,1). \det H = 1: the area is unchanged.
B2. (a) \det = 1: twice as wide, half as tall, area unchanged, not mirrored. (b) \det = -1: mirrored left–right, area unchanged. (c) \det = 1: a rotation by 180°, not a mirror image. (d) \det = 0.5 - 0.5 = 0: the columns are parallel, the whole image is squashed onto a line; area 0, not invertible.
B3. A^{-1} = \tfrac12 I, so \mathbf{x} = A^{-1}\mathbf{x}' = (1.5, 2.5): between pixels, so we must interpolate.
B4. Along x at y = 0: 10 + 0.25\,(20 - 10) = 12.5. At y = 1: 30 + 0.25\,(60 - 30) = 37.5. Along y: 12.5 + 0.5\,(37.5 - 12.5) = 25. Nearest neighbour: (0.25, 0.5) is equally far from (0, 0) and (0, 1), so it depends on the tie-breaking rule: 10 or 30. (Rounding 0.5 up gives (0, 1), value 30.)
B5. (3, 1): shifted, it is (1, 0), one step to the right of \mathbf{p}; a quarter turn takes it to (0, 1); shifting back gives (2, 2), one step above \mathbf{p}. (2, 3): shifted, (0, 2); turned, (-2, 0); shifted back, (0, 1), two steps to the left of \mathbf{p}. The point \mathbf{p} itself stays where it is.
B6. S then R: (1, 0) \to (2, 0) \to (0, 2). R then S: (1, 0) \to (0, 1) \to (0, 1): the stretch along x no longer touches it, because it now points up. The square stretched first becomes wide, then the quarter turn stands it up: tall (twice as tall as wide). Turned first, it is still a square, then stretched along x: wide. The two orders give different images, so the order of transforms matters.




Math questions
B7. (math) Write the 3\times3 homogeneous matrix that rotates by 90° counter-clockwise about the point \mathbf{p} = (2, 1), as a product T_{\mathbf{p}}\,R\,T_{-\mathbf{p}}. Check it: where does \mathbf{p} go? Where does (3, 1) go? Compare with B5.
B8. (math) Show that in bilinear interpolation it does not matter whether you interpolate along x first (as in B4) or along y first: both give (1-\alpha)(1-\beta)\,I_{00} + \alpha(1-\beta)\,I_{10} + (1-\alpha)\beta\,I_{01} + \alpha\beta\,I_{11} at the point (\alpha, \beta). Check it on the numbers of B4, interpolating along y first.






Solutions (math)





B7. T_{\mathbf{p}}RT_{-\mathbf{p}} =
\begin{bmatrix}1&0&2\\0&1&1\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}0&-1&0\\1&0&0\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}1&0&-2\\0&1&-1\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}
= \begin{bmatrix}0&-1&3\\1&0&-1\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}. Check: (2, 1) \mapsto (0\cdot2 - 1 + 3,\; 2 + 0 - 1) = (2, 1), so \mathbf{p} stays fixed. (3, 1) \mapsto (-1 + 3,\; 3 - 1) = (2, 2): the point one step to the right of \mathbf{p} ends up one step above it, a quarter turn counter-clockwise, as in B5.
B8. Along x first: the two rows give (1-\alpha)I_{00} + \alpha I_{10} and (1-\alpha)I_{01} + \alpha I_{11}; interpolating these along y with weights 1-\beta and \beta gives the four terms above. Along y first: the two columns give (1-\beta)I_{00} + \beta I_{01} and (1-\beta)I_{10} + \beta I_{11}; interpolating along x with weights 1-\alpha and \alpha gives the same four products, in a different order. With the numbers of B4 (\alpha = 0.25, \beta = 0.5): along y at x = 0: 10 + 0.5\,(30 - 10) = 20; at x = 1: 20 + 0.5\,(60 - 20) = 40; then along x: 20 + 0.25\,(40 - 20) = 25, the same as before.

title: Exercise: images as arrays & geometric transforms
text:
Explore
The same ideas on a picture: a drawn cell (with an “F” in the corner, so mirror images are easy to spot), centred on the origin. Drag the red and blue handles (the columns of A) or use the presets and the rotation slider.



E1. Drag the blue handle to make the shear H from B1. Does the frame (solid outline) look like your sketch?
E2. Before clicking, predict each preset from its columns: Rotate 30°, Scale, Reflect, Misaligned. Which one gives a mirror image? Then set the rotation slider to 180°: is that a mirror image too?
E3. Click Collapse, then slowly drag the blue handle away from the red one. When exactly does the cell become a line?
E4. Click Scale and look closely at the edges of the cell and the F. The demo uses nearest-neighbour lookup. What would bilinear interpolation change?






Solutions





E1. The red handle stays at (1, 0); put the blue one at (2, 1). Horizontal lines stay horizontal and every point slides sideways by 2 times its height: the x-axis stays put, the top edge of the frame (height 1.5) slides 3 units to the right and the bottom edge 3 units to the left, so the corners leave the view. The lean is the same as in the B1 sketch, where the top of the unit square (height 1) slides 2 units.
E2. Rotate 30°: columns (0.87, 0.5) and (-0.5, 0.87), the picture turns counter-clockwise. Scale: columns (2, 0) and (0, 0.5), twice as wide, half as tall. Reflect: column 1 is (-1, 0), so the picture is mirrored left–right and the F reads backwards. Misaligned: tilted and skewed, as two images of the same sample often are before registration. Rotating by 180° turns the F upside down, but it is not a mirror image: turn your head (or the screen) and it reads normally again. Only the reflection flips it (\det = -1).
E3. Exactly when the two columns lie on one line through the origin, i.e. when \det A = 0. Then every point x\cdot\text{col 1} + y\cdot\text{col 2} is on that line, so the whole picture is squashed onto it. As soon as the columns point in different directions, the picture is a (thin) parallelogram again.
E4. In the horizontal direction each input pixel now covers two output pixels, so edges look blocky and staircase-like. Bilinear interpolation would blend neighbouring values, giving smooth ramps instead of steps, at the price of introducing grey levels that were not in the input (bad for label images, where every value is an object ID).

title: Graph-cut segmentation
text:
About this lecture
Two units ago: segmentation = minimise E(L) = \sum_p D_p(L_p) + \lambda \sum_{(p,q)} w_{pq}[L_p \ne L_q]. Last unit: minimum cuts by max-flow. Today we connect them (Boykov & Jolly, 2001).

Build a graph from an image so that cut cost = energy.
One max-flow gives the exact best segmentation.
Contrast-sensitive weights: boundaries are cheap at image edges.
Seeds: the user marks some object and background pixels.
What goes wrong: shrinking, blocky boundaries, a bad intensity model.

Slides titled The math give the formulas and proofs; the ideas are complete without them.

title: Graph-cut segmentation
text:
The graph
One node per pixel, plus s (= object) and t (= background). A pixel on the source side gets L_p = 1.

t-links (to the terminals) carry the data term:

s \to p with capacity D_p(0): cut when p ends up on the background side;
p \to t with capacity D_p(1): cut when p ends up on the object side.

n-links between neighbours carry the smoothness term: p \to q and q \to p, each with capacity \lambda w_{pq}.

Every pixel loses exactly one of its two t-links in any cut: the one that matches its label’s cost.

title: Graph-cut segmentation
text:
Cut cost = energy
Take any s–t cut and read off L_p = 1 for p \in S, L_p = 0 for p \in T.

Pixel p \in S: its edge p \to t crosses from S to T and costs D_p(1); s \to p stays inside S.
Pixel p \in T: s \to p crosses and costs D_p(0).
Neighbours with L_p = L_q: no n-link crosses. With L_p = 1, L_q = 0: only p \to q crosses, cost \lambda w_{pq}.

c(S, T) = \sum_p D_p(L_p) + \lambda \sum_{(p,q)} w_{pq}[L_p \ne L_q] = E(L).
Every labelling is a cut and every cut a labelling, at the same cost: minimum cut = minimum energy.

title: Graph-cut segmentation
section: The math: which energies can be cut?
text:
The math: which energies can be cut?

Capacities must be \ge 0. If D_p(0) or D_p(1) is negative, add the same constant to both: every labelling changes by the same amount.
The pairwise term must be submodular (Kolmogorov & Zabih, 2004): V(0,1) + V(1,0) \ge V(0,0) + V(1,1). The boundary term \lambda w_{pq}[L_p \ne L_q] is \lambda w_{pq} + \lambda w_{pq} \ge 0 + 0: fine.
Then the minimum is exact, global, in polynomial time.
Not covered: more than two labels. The Potts energy with 3 or more labels is NP-hard; α-expansion solves a sequence of two-label cuts and gets within a factor 2.

title: Graph-cut segmentation
text:
Contrast-sensitive weights
Make boundaries cheap where the image changes:
w_{pq} = \exp\!\left(-\frac{(I_p - I_q)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)

Equal neighbours: w_{pq} = 1, a full boundary cost \lambda.
Very different neighbours: w_{pq} \approx 0, cutting there is almost free.
\sigma sets what counts as “very different”: about the size of the intensity jump at a real edge, larger than the noise.
\sigma = \infty gives w_{pq} = 1: the boundary length alone.

The 1\times 3 example with \sigma = 1: |I_1 - I_2| = 2, so w = e^{-2} = 0.135. Now 101 costs 1 + 2\lambda \cdot 0.135: thresholding wins up to \lambda = 11.1.

title: Graph-cut segmentation
section: Try it: the graph of a small image
text:
Try it: the graph of a small image




Grey levels 0 to 3, data costs I² (to s) and (3 − I)² (to t). Small images show the whole graph with every capacity; the dashed red edges are the minimum cut, and the table checks that the cut equals the energy and the max flow. Tour: 1 × 3 at λ = 1: cut 3, labelling 101. Move λ past 1.5: 111 wins. Set σ to 1: the n-links around the dark pixel become thin (0.135) and 101 comes back. Then 2 × 2, and “label (your cut)”: click pixels to choose your own cut and compare its cost with the minimum. Finally “thin vs thick” (6 × 6): raise λ; the 1-pixel line disappears at 1.5, the 3-pixel band only at 9. Shrinking bias in miniature.

title: Graph-cut segmentation
text:
Seeds
The user paints a few object and background pixels (Boykov & Jolly, 2001):

Hard constraints: an object seed gets s \to p with capacity “\infty” (larger than any possible cut), so it can never be on the background side. Background seeds likewise with p \to t.
Intensity model from the seeds: fit a Gaussian, or take a histogram, of the seed pixels of each label; D_p(\ell) = -\log P(I_p \mid \ell).
Interactive: look at the result, add a seed where it is wrong, cut again. A new max-flow takes milliseconds at this size.

Thresholding with the same model (\lambda = 0) is the baseline to beat.

title: Graph-cut segmentation
text:
Try it: interactive graph cut




128 × 128 image; paint with the mouse (object = red, background = blue). The left image shows the graph-cut result (yellow boundary), the small one thresholding with the same intensity model. Tour: “noise” (λ = 1.5): thresholding has 2587 wrong pixels, the graph cut 55, and the thin arm survives. Raise λ: at about 1.7 half the arm goes, at 4.7 nearly all of it (“thin arm lost”). “Blocky”: with 4 neighbours the disk comes out as a rounded square; switch to 8 neighbours. “Nucleus”: histogram model, contrast weights σ = 25; there is a leak at the right edge: paint a background seed there. “Overlapping intensities”: background seeds only on the white areas, so the cytoplasm looks like nucleus and is included.

title: Graph-cut segmentation
text:
Failure modes

Shrinking bias: the boundary term grows with length. A thin structure has a long boundary for its area: its data gain \propto area, its boundary cost \propto length. A strip of width k survives only if its data gain per pixel exceeds about 2\lambda/k.
Metrication: with 4 neighbours a boundary costs its length in the “city-block” metric: a diagonal boundary costs \sqrt2 = 1.41 per unit length, a horizontal one 1. The cut prefers axis-aligned, blocky shapes. With 8 neighbours and weights \tfrac12 (sides) and \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt2} (diagonals), both cost \tfrac12 + \tfrac{1}{\sqrt2} = 1.21 per unit length.
Overlapping intensities: if object and background have the same grey levels, no data term can separate them; only seeds and image edges can.

title: Graph-cut segmentation
text:
Beyond: GrabCut and more labels

GrabCut (Rother, Kolmogorov & Blake, 2004): colour images, the user draws only a box. Alternate: fit colour models (mixtures of Gaussians) to the current labelling, cut again, until it settles.
More than two labels (several tissues, several cells): α-expansion repeats binary cuts, “label \alpha or keep your label”, over all labels.
The same graph construction appears in stereo matching, image stitching and denoising: any energy with unary and submodular pairwise terms.

title: Graph-cut segmentation
text:
Summary

Graph: pixels + s (object) + t (background); t-links = data term, n-links = \lambda w_{pq}.
Cut cost = energy, so one max-flow gives the exact minimum of a submodular binary energy.
Contrast weights w_{pq} = e^{-(I_p - I_q)^2/2\sigma^2} pull the boundary onto image edges.
Seeds: hard constraints by infinite t-links, and the intensity model.
Watch for shrinking bias, metrication (use 8 neighbours) and overlapping intensity models.

title: Quiz: images in frequency space
text:
Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

Q1. Why does the discrete Fourier transform lose no information about an image?






Answer





It is a change of basis: X = Fx with an invertible matrix F (F^{-1} = \tfrac1N F^*, because the waves are orthogonal). The image and its spectrum are the same vector written in two bases, and x = F^{-1}X recovers the image exactly.




Q2. In the centred spectrum of a micrograph, where do you find the information about (a) the overall brightness, (b) the broad shape of the cell, (c) the fine texture and the noise?






Answer






The single centre coefficient, frequency (0, 0): it is N^2 times the mean grey level. (b) Close to the centre: low frequencies. (c) Far from the centre: high frequencies. Note that sharp real edges are high-frequency as well, so a low-pass filter that removes noise also blurs edges.





Q3. An image has a regular pattern of horizontal stripes (lines running left–right), 8 pixels apart, in a 256 × 256 image. Where are the bright dots in its spectrum?






Hint





The brightness changes when you move up and down, not left–right. How many cycles fit in the image?









Answer





On the vertical axis through the centre, at 256/8 = 32 cycles: the pair (u, v) = (0, \pm 32). The dots are perpendicular to the stripes, and come in a mirror pair because the image is real.




Q4. You blur an image by convolving with a 31 \times 31 Gaussian kernel. How else could you compute the same result, and why might it be faster?






Answer





By the convolution theorem: FFT the image and the (zero-padded) kernel, multiply the spectra, inverse FFT. Direct convolution costs about 31^2 \approx 960 multiplications per pixel; the FFT route costs \mathcal{O}(\log N) per pixel. (The Gaussian is also separable: a 31-tap pass along rows then along columns, 62 multiplications per pixel.) Beware: the FFT treats the image as periodic, so pad the image to avoid wrap-around at the border.




Q5. You reduce a photo of a brick wall to a quarter of its size by keeping every 4th pixel in each direction. A strange wavy pattern appears that is not on the wall. What happened, and how do you prevent it?






Answer





Aliasing. The new grid can only hold frequencies up to a quarter of the original Nyquist frequency; the fine brick pattern is above that and folds back as a false, coarser pattern (moiré). Low-pass filter (blur) the image first, so that what the coarse grid cannot represent is removed before sampling.




Q6. A detector adds a faint regular stripe to every image. Should you remove it with a low-pass filter or a notch filter? Why?






Answer





A notch. The stripe is a single wave, so in the spectrum it is one isolated pair of dots; zeroing just those (and their immediate neighbours) removes the stripe and leaves everything else. A low-pass filter would also remove every real structure finer than the stripe.

title: Exercise: images in frequency space
text:
By hand
B1. (Orthogonality.) Show that for integers m, n \ge 1, \int_0^1 \sin(2\pi m t)\,\sin(2\pi n t)\,dt = \begin{cases} 0 & m \ne n,\\ \tfrac12 & m = n.\end{cases} (Use \sin a \sin b = \tfrac12[\cos(a - b) - \cos(a + b)].) If f(t) = \sum_n a_n \sin(2\pi n t), how do you get a_3 back from f?
B2. Compute the DFT X_k = \sum_{n=0}^{3} x_n e^{-2\pi i kn/4} of x = (1, 0, -1, 0) for k = 0, 1, 2, 3. Which wave is x? Why are there two non-zero coefficients for a single wave?
B3. Show that for a real signal x, X_{N-k} = \overline{X_k}. Use this to explain why a single stripe pattern in an image gives a pair of dots in its 2D spectrum, mirrored through the centre.
B4. (Shift theorem.) Let y_n = x_{n-m} (indices modulo N: the signal is shifted by m and wraps around). Show that Y_k = e^{-2\pi i km/N}\, X_k. What happens to |X_k|, and what to the phase? What does this mean for the magnitude spectrum of a cell that moves within the image?
B5. (Frequency response.) Filtering with the 1D kernel w = (w_{-1}, w_0, w_1) multiplies the wave e^{i\omega n} by \hat w(\omega) = w_{-1}e^{-i\omega} + w_0 + w_1 e^{i\omega}. Compute \hat w(\omega) for

the blur \tfrac14(1, 2, 1) and (b) the second difference (1, -2, 1).

Evaluate both at \omega = 0 (a constant signal) and \omega = \pi (the fastest wave the grid can hold: +1, -1, +1, \dots). Which is low-pass, which high-pass? Relate \hat w(0) to the sum of the weights.






Solutions





B1. \sin(2\pi m t)\sin(2\pi n t) = \tfrac12[\cos 2\pi(m-n)t - \cos 2\pi(m+n)t]. Over one period, \int_0^1 \cos(2\pi j t)\,dt = 0 for any integer j \neq 0 and = 1 for j = 0. If m \ne n both terms integrate to 0. If m = n, the first term is \tfrac12 \cdot 1 and the second 0, giving \tfrac12. So, multiplying f by \sin(2\pi \cdot 3 t) and integrating kills every term except n = 3: a_3 = 2\int_0^1 f(t)\sin(6\pi t)\,dt. This is a projection onto one basis vector.
B2. e^{-2\pi i k n/4} = (-i)^{kn}, and only n = 0 and n = 2 contribute: X_k = 1 - (-i)^{2k} = 1 - (-1)^k. So X = (0, 2, 0, 2). The signal x_n = \cos(2\pi n/4) is one cycle of a cosine. Since \cos\theta = \tfrac12(e^{i\theta} + e^{-i\theta}), it is made of frequency +1 and frequency -1, and index k = 3 = N - 1 is frequency -1.
B3. X_{N-k} = \sum_n x_n e^{-2\pi i (N-k)n/N} = \sum_n x_n e^{-2\pi i n}\, e^{2\pi i kn/N} = \sum_n x_n e^{2\pi i kn/N}, since e^{-2\pi i n} = 1. For real x_n this is the complex conjugate of X_k. A real stripe pattern is a cosine wave, which needs both e^{+i\theta} and e^{-i\theta}: frequencies (u, v) and (-u, -v), a pair of dots mirrored through the centre, with equal magnitude.
B4. Y_k = \sum_n x_{n-m} e^{-2\pi i kn/N}. Substitute p = n - m (the sum runs over all residues modulo N either way): Y_k = \sum_p x_p e^{-2\pi i k(p+m)/N} = e^{-2\pi i km/N} X_k. The factor has modulus 1, so |Y_k| = |X_k|: the magnitude is unchanged and only the phase changes, by -2\pi km/N. The magnitude spectrum of an image does not depend on where the cell is: it describes what structures are present, not where. (This is why the magnitude spectrum is useful as a texture feature, and also why the phase cannot be thrown away when rebuilding an image.)
B5. (a) \hat w(\omega) = \tfrac14(e^{-i\omega} + 2 + e^{i\omega}) = \tfrac14(2 + 2\cos\omega) = \tfrac12(1 + \cos\omega). \hat w(0) = 1: constants pass unchanged. \hat w(\pi) = 0: the fastest wave is removed completely. Low-pass. (b) \hat w(\omega) = e^{-i\omega} - 2 + e^{i\omega} = 2\cos\omega - 2 = -4\sin^2(\omega/2). \hat w(0) = 0: constants are removed. \hat w(\pi) = -4: the fastest wave is amplified 4 times (and flipped). High-pass; for small \omega, \hat w \approx -\omega^2, the frequency response of a second derivative (\tfrac{d^2}{dt^2}e^{i\omega t} = -\omega^2 e^{i\omega t}). In both cases \hat w(0) = \sum w, the sum of the weights.

title: Exercise: images in frequency space
text:
Explore: build a wave
The demo below adds up five waves, a_f \sin(2\pi f\,t) for f = 1, \dots, 5 cycles per window, over one window 0 \le t \le 1. Each slider sets one amplitude a_f and has the same colour as its thin line in the plot; the bold black line is the sum. (A sine is a cosine with phase \varphi = -\pi/2.) The bar chart shows the amplitude spectrum |a_f|: the amount of each frequency, which is what the Fourier transform of the black curve gives back.



W1. Choose pure tone. How many cycles does the sum complete in the window, and what does the spectrum look like? Now set that slider to −1. What changes in the plot, and what changes in the spectrum? Which of the three sinusoid parameters (frequency, amplitude, phase) did the sign change?
W2. Start from all zero, set a_1 = 1, then add a_3 \approx 0.33 and finally a_5 = 0.2 (or press square). Describe how the shape of the sum changes at each step. Roughly what height do the flat parts reach? Which frequencies would you have to add to make the edges steeper still?
W3. Press sawtooth and compare its spectrum with the one for square. Then change the signs of a_2 and a_4 to +1/2 and +1/4. What happens to the signal, and to the spectrum? (Compare with B4.) Finally, change only a_3 to -1/3. Does the signal still have the same shape? What information does the amplitude spectrum leave out?






Solutions





W1. The pure tone is \sin(2\pi\cdot 2\cdot t): two cycles in the window, and a single bar at f = 2 of height 1. With amplitude −1 the wave is flipped upside down, which is the same as sliding it half a cycle along: the phase changed by \pi. Frequency and the height |a| are the same, so the amplitude spectrum does not change.
W2. a_1 alone is one smooth swell. Adding the third harmonic flattens the tops and steepens the sides; adding the fifth flattens them further, with small ripples on the plateaus. The flat parts sit near \pm\pi/4 \approx \pm 0.79 (that is the limit of \sin x + \tfrac13\sin 3x + \tfrac15\sin 5x + \dots; with three terms the plateaus wiggle around this value). Steeper edges need higher odd harmonics: f = 7, 9, 11, \dots with amplitudes 1/7, 1/9, \dots. Sharp edges live at high frequencies.
W3. The square wave uses only the odd frequencies; the sawtooth uses all five, with heights 1, 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5. Flipping the signs of a_2 and a_4 gives the same sawtooth, moved by half a window: shifting t by 1/2 multiplies \sin(2\pi f t) by (-1)^f, so it flips exactly the even frequencies. The spectrum is unchanged, as in B4: a time shift changes the phases, not the amplitudes. Flipping only a_3 is not a shift: the signal gets a clearly different shape, yet the bars are still the same. The amplitude spectrum leaves out the phase of each wave (here only its sign), so different signals can share the same amplitude spectrum. The full Fourier transform keeps the phase too, which is why the signal can be rebuilt from it.

title: Exercise: images in frequency space
text:
Explore: filter an image
The demo below is the lecture’s micrograph (a 256 × 256 crop). Left: the image; middle: its 2D spectrum, log of the magnitude, with frequency 0 in the centre; right: the image rebuilt from the coefficients you keep. Removed coefficients are shown dark red. The radial filters keep the coefficients whose distance r from the centre lies between a min radius and a max radius (the two blue circles; ∞ means no upper limit). The buttons are presets: low-pass sets min = 0, high-pass sets max = ∞, band-pass uses both. The box “keep average brightness (centre)” keeps the centre coefficient whatever the min radius is. The readout gives the share of coefficients kept, the share of the image’s variation they carry, and the RMS error of the rebuilt image (pixel values run from 0 to 1).



E1. Choose low-pass (min radius 0) and set the max radius to 5, 30 and 90. For each, note the percentage of coefficients kept and the percentage of the variation kept. What does that tell you about where the image’s content sits in the spectrum?
E2. Choose keep largest at 3%. Then go back to low-pass and find the max radius that also keeps about 3% of the coefficients. Which of the two has the smaller error? Look at where the kept coefficients lie in the spectrum in “keep largest” mode: why are the two results so similar?
E3. Choose high-pass (max radius ∞) with min radius 10. What is left of the cell? Why is the picture grey rather than black, although most of the low frequencies are gone? Untick keep average brightness (centre) to check your answer.
E4. Tick add stripe artefact and choose no filter: note the error. The stripe adds two bright coefficients to the spectrum, marked with yellow rings. Erase them by dragging over them. What happens to the error? Why are there two dots for one stripe? Then try removing the stripe with a low-pass filter instead, at max radius 15. Which approach is better here?
E5. Go back to low-pass with max radius 30, then raise the min radius from 0 to 5, so that only a ring between the two circles is kept. How many coefficients does that remove, and how much of the variation? What disappears from the image, and what is left? Compare with E1.






Solutions





E1. Radius 5 keeps 0.12% of the coefficients but already 53% of the variation; radius 30 keeps 4.3% of the coefficients and 81% of the variation; radius 90 keeps 39% and 96%. A tiny disc of low frequencies carries most of the variation: the broad light and dark regions. The many high-frequency coefficients each carry little; together they make the fine detail (and the grain). This is why a frequency basis compresses natural images well.
E2. Keep largest 3%: 81% of the variation, RMS error 0.100. Low-pass with max radius 25 also keeps 3.0% of the coefficients: 78% of the variation, error 0.109. Keeping the largest coefficients is slightly better, because it picks the coefficients that matter for this image, while the disc is fixed in advance. They are similar because most of the largest coefficients are low frequencies anyway: in “keep largest” mode the kept coefficients crowd around the centre, with a scatter of single ones further out.
E3. Only edges and fine texture remain: the outline of the nucleus, the membranes, the grain inside the cell. Large uniform regions all become the same grey, because their brightness is low-frequency content. The picture stays grey because the centre coefficient (frequency 0, the average brightness of the whole image) is kept by the “keep average brightness” box, even though it lies inside the min radius. Untick the box and the average of the rebuilt image drops from 0.66 to 0: the values vary around 0, the negative half is shown as black (about half the pixels), and the RMS error jumps from 0.18 to 0.69.
E4. With the stripe and no filter the error is 0.106 (the stripe itself). The stripe is a single 2D wave, so it adds a single bright pair of coefficients, about 19 units from the centre (16 across, 10 down, and its mirror image). Erasing them brings the error down to about 0.02; zeroing exactly the two coefficients would give 0.002, the brush also removes a few of the cell’s own coefficients around them. There are two dots because a real-valued wave is the sum of a frequency and its mirror image (+k and -k), the mirror symmetry of B3. A low-pass filter at max radius 15 also removes the stripe, but it removes the cell’s detail too: the error is 0.127, worse than leaving the stripe in. A notch removes exactly what you want to remove; a low-pass removes everything above a frequency.
E5. Raising the min radius from 0 to 5 removes very few coefficients: the kept share drops from 4.3% to 4.2% (only 68 of the 65 536 coefficients lie inside radius 5, not counting the centre, which is kept). But the variation kept drops from 81% to 29%, and the RMS error rises from 0.10 to 0.19. As in E1, the few lowest frequencies carry about half of the variation: they are the broad shading, such as the dark nucleus against the lighter cytoplasm. Without them the nucleus becomes the same mid grey as its surroundings, and what is left is structure of intermediate size: the outline of the nucleus, membranes and small organelles, but neither the overall shading (below the min radius) nor the fine grain (above the max radius). A band-pass picks out structures of one size range.

title: Exercise: images in frequency space
text:
Where this leads
Frequency-space features (peaks, orientation, texture energy in a ring) are a classic input for classifying textures. Larger blurs at many scales (a scale space) and the Laplacian of Gaussian come back when we detect objects.

title: Quiz: from PCA to autoencoders
text:
Short questions on encoders, decoders and PCA. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. An encoder maps an image to a few numbers z; a decoder maps z back to an image; an autoencoder trains both so that decode(encode(image)) is close to the image.

Q1. In one sentence each: what does the encoder do, what does the decoder do, and what is an autoencoder trained to achieve?






Hint





Think of the hourglass: wide, narrow, wide.









Answer





The encoder compresses an image into a few numbers z (its place in the latent space). The decoder rebuilds the whole image from z alone. Both are trained together so that the rebuilt image is as close as possible to the input, for many images at once.




Q2. PCA with one component, PC1 = (0.6,\ 0.8), a two-pixel image with the mean subtracted, \mathbf x = (1,\ 2). Encode, decode, and give the squared reconstruction error.






Hint





Encode = dot product with PC1. Decode = score × PC1.









Answer





Score = 0.6 + 1.6 = 2.2. Decoded 2.2 \cdot (0.6,\ 0.8) = (1.32,\ 1.76). Error (-0.32,\ 0.24), squared length 0.1024 + 0.0576 = 0.16.




Q3. Why must the bottleneck be narrow? What would an autoencoder with a 784-number bottleneck learn on 28\times28 images?






Hint





What is the cheapest way to make the output equal the input?









Answer





With a bottleneck as wide as the input it can pass the image straight through (or rotate it and rotate it back, as PCA with all components does). The reconstruction is perfect but z summarises nothing. A narrow bottleneck forces z to keep only the main ways in which the images differ.




Q4. For the same data, which has the smaller reconstruction error with 2 numbers per image: PCA, or a trained autoencoder whose encoder and decoder have no ReLU?






Hint





What is a network without bends?









Answer





They are (at best) equal. Without bends, encoder and decoder are linear maps, and among linear encoder/decoder pairs with 2 numbers PCA already has the smallest squared error. Only the bends let an autoencoder beat PCA.




Q5. Images of a cell that slowly elongates lie on a curve in pixel space. Why can a nonlinear autoencoder describe them with one number, where PCA needs several?






Hint





Straight line or curve?









Answer





PCA decodes along straight lines (flat subspaces), so a curved family needs several directions to hold its bends. A nonlinear decoder maps one number to a curve, which can follow the family: one number says how far along the elongation the cell is.




Q6. In a 28\times28 PCA, what does a principal component look like if you display it?






Hint





How many entries does it have?









Answer





It has 784 entries, so it can be shown as a 28\times28 image (an “eigen-image”), with positive and negative values. Decoding adds the mean image and the eigen-images weighted by the scores.

title: Exercise: from PCA to autoencoders
text:
Background







Word
Meaning




Image as a vector
the grey values, one after the other: a 28\times28 image is a point in \mathbb R^{784}


Mean image \bar{\mathbf x}
the pixel-wise average of all images


Principal component \mathbf u_k
a unit vector (itself an image, an “eigen-image”); \mathbf u_1 points along the largest spread


Encode (PCA)
scores s_k = \mathbf u_k \cdot (\mathbf x - \bar{\mathbf x})


Decode (PCA)
\hat{\mathbf x} = \bar{\mathbf x} + s_1\mathbf u_1 + \dots + s_k\mathbf u_k


Reconstruction error
\|\mathbf x - \hat{\mathbf x}\|^2, the squared length of what is lost


Autoencoder
encoder and decoder are neural networks; trained so that \hat{\mathbf x} \approx \mathbf x

title: Exercise: from PCA to autoencoders
text:
By hand

Part A — PCA as an encoder and a decoder
Two-pixel images, mean already subtracted. PC1 is \mathbf u = (0.8,\ 0.6), a unit vector.
B1. Encode \mathbf x = (3,\ 1): compute its score. Decode it again. What is the reconstruction error vector, and its squared length?
B2. Do the same for \mathbf y = (-1.6,\ -1.2) and \mathbf w = (-0.6,\ 0.8). Which one is rebuilt perfectly, and which one is rebuilt as the mean image (0, 0)? Explain both with the PC1 line.
B3. Now keep two components, with PC2 = (-0.6,\ 0.8). What is the reconstruction error of \mathbf x now? What does that say about an autoencoder whose bottleneck is as wide as its input?


Part B — brightness and edges
Two neighbouring pixels of a smooth image. The mean image is (0.5,\ 0.5), PC1 is \mathbf u_1 = (1, 1)/\sqrt2 and PC2 is \mathbf u_2 = (1, -1)/\sqrt2.
B4. Describe in words what \mathbf u_1 and \mathbf u_2 look like as two-pixel images, and what their scores measure.
B5. Encode the image (0.8,\ 0.6) with one component and decode it. What is lost? Give the error. What is the score on PC2?
B6. A 28\times28 image is encoded by PCA with 50 components. How many numbers are stored per image? What does the decoder add up to rebuild the image?


Part C — curved families
B7. A bright spot moves past two pixels (the lecture’s horseshoe). Explain in your own words why one PCA score cannot tell all spot positions apart, while one autoencoder number can.
B8. An autoencoder with no ReLU in its networks is trained on images. What will it find? (Use the collapse argument of Neural networks.)
B9 (math). Let S be the covariance matrix of centred data \mathbf y_i and \mathbf u a unit vector. Show that the mean squared error of the one-number linear autoencoder along \mathbf u is \operatorname{tr}S - \mathbf u^\top S\mathbf u. For S = \begin{pmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{pmatrix}, compute this error for \mathbf u = (1, 0) and for \mathbf u = (1, 1)/\sqrt2, and find the best \mathbf u.






Solutions





B1. Score = 0.8 \cdot 3 + 0.6 \cdot 1 = 3.0. Decoded 3.0 \cdot (0.8, 0.6) = (2.4,\ 1.8). Error (3, 1) - (2.4, 1.8) = (0.6,\ -0.8), squared length 0.36 + 0.64 = 1.0.
B2. \mathbf y: score = -1.28 - 0.72 = -2.0, decoded (-1.6,\ -1.2) = \mathbf y: error 0. \mathbf y lies on the PC1 line, so nothing is lost. \mathbf w: score = -0.48 + 0.48 = 0, decoded (0, 0), the mean image; error 0.36 + 0.64 = 1.0. \mathbf w is perpendicular to PC1: its one number carries no information about it.
B3. Scores 3.0 and -0.6 \cdot 3 + 0.8 \cdot 1 = -1.0. Decoded 3.0\,(0.8, 0.6) - 1.0\,(-0.6, 0.8) = (2.4 + 0.6,\ 1.8 - 0.8) = (3, 1): error 0. With as many numbers as pixels, encoding is a rotation and decoding rotates back. Nothing is lost, but nothing is summarised either: the bottleneck has to be narrower than the input to be useful.
B4. \mathbf u_1: both pixels equally bright, the score measures the overall brightness of the pair. \mathbf u_2: one pixel brighter, the other darker by the same amount, the score measures the difference, a tiny edge.
B5. \mathbf x - \bar{\mathbf x} = (0.3,\ 0.1). Score s_1 = (0.3 + 0.1)/\sqrt2 = 0.2828. Decoded \bar{\mathbf x} + s_1\mathbf u_1 = (0.5, 0.5) + (0.2, 0.2) = (0.7,\ 0.7). Error (0.1,\ -0.1), squared length 0.02. The edge between the two pixels is lost; its score on PC2 is (0.3 - 0.1)/\sqrt2 = 0.1414, and 0.1414^2 = 0.02 is exactly the lost error.
B6. 50 scores per image instead of 784 grey values. The decoder adds the mean image and 50 eigen-images, each multiplied by its score.
B7. One PCA score is a position along one straight line. The images of the moving spot lie on a bent curve, so when the curve is projected onto a line it folds: two different spot positions (for example -0.5 and 0.2) project to almost the same score, and the decoder must give them the same image. An autoencoder’s decoder is a curve, not a line: one number says where along the curve the image is, and different positions get different numbers.
B8. Without bends, the encoder is one matrix and the decoder is one matrix (plus shifts): a linear autoencoder. Trained on squared error, the best it can do is PCA: its decoder spans the same directions as the top principal components.
B9 (math). For a unit \mathbf u, \mathbf y = (\mathbf u^\top\mathbf y)\mathbf u + \mathbf r with \mathbf r \perp \mathbf u, so by Pythagoras \|\mathbf r\|^2 = \|\mathbf y\|^2 - (\mathbf u^\top\mathbf y)^2. Averaging over the data: \frac1n\sum\|\mathbf y_i\|^2 = \operatorname{tr}S and \frac1n\sum(\mathbf u^\top\mathbf y_i)^2 = \mathbf u^\top S\mathbf u. For the given S: \operatorname{tr}S = 4. \mathbf u = (1, 0): \mathbf u^\top S\mathbf u = 2, error 2. \mathbf u = (1, 1)/\sqrt2: \mathbf u^\top S\mathbf u = (2 + 1 + 1 + 2)/2 = 3, error 1. The eigenvalues of S are 3 (eigenvector (1,1)/\sqrt2) and 1 (eigenvector (1,-1)/\sqrt2); \mathbf u^\top S\mathbf u \le 3 for every unit vector, so (1,1)/\sqrt2 is best, with error equal to the dropped eigenvalue, 1.

title: Exercise: from PCA to autoencoders
text:
Explore
Each dot is a two-pixel image (pixel 1 across, pixel 2 up). The blue line through the mean is a linear autoencoder that keeps one number: drag the handle u to turn it. Red segments join each image to its reconstruction. The small plot shows the mean squared error for every angle of \mathbf u; PCA jumps to the best angle. Click a dot to see that image and its reconstructions as two grey squares. On moving spot, train nonlinear autoencoder trains a 2 \to 16 \to 1 \to 16 \to 2 network (fixed seed) and draws its decoder curve in green.



E1. At the start, \mathbf u points along pixel 1 (angle 0°). What does this encoder keep, and what does the decoder do with pixel 2? Read the error. Check it against the readout’s “keep nothing” error and the covariance in the lecture’s math slide, if you did it.
E2. Turn \mathbf u slowly through all angles. At which angle is the error smallest, and at which largest? Press PCA to check. What do the two directions mean for a pair of neighbouring pixels?
E3. With PCA selected, click a few dots. Compare the image and its linear reconstruction as grey squares: what is always lost?
E4. Choose moving spot, then spot: PCA. Where are the red segments longest? Find two dots far apart along the curve that land on almost the same point of the line.
E5. Press train nonlinear autoencoder. Watch the green curve during training. Compare its final error with the PCA error. Why is the curve still one-dimensional (one number per image)?






Solutions





E1. At 0° the score is pixel 1 minus its mean: the encoder keeps pixel 1 and throws pixel 2 away. The decoder rebuilds pixel 1 exactly and sets pixel 2 to its mean, 0.511 (for the selected image (0.439, 0.466) it gives (0.439, 0.511)). Error 0.0414, half of the “keep nothing” error 0.0820. In the math: \operatorname{tr}S - S_{11} = 0.0820 - 0.0406 = 0.0414.
E2. Smallest at 45.3° (error 0.0058, the PCA direction): both pixels together, the brightness. Largest at −45° (0.0762): keeping only the difference of the two pixels and losing the brightness. Neighbouring pixels mostly differ in overall brightness from pair to pair, much less from each other.
E3. The reconstruction always has two (almost) equally bright pixels: the small difference between them, the local edge, is lost. Images that already have equal pixels are rebuilt almost perfectly.
E4. PCA error 0.0170. The red segments are longest at the two ends of the horseshoe (spot far left or far right, both pixels fairly dark), where the curve bends back towards the mean and is furthest from the line. The images at the start of the curve (spot far left, pixel 1 medium, pixel 2 dark) and those a little past pixel 1 (pixel 1 bright, pixel 2 a bit brighter) project to nearby points of the line: the line folds the curve.
E5. After 1500 steps the error is 0.0006, against 0.0170 for PCA: almost thirty times smaller. The green curve starts roughly straight and bends during training until it follows the horseshoe. It is still one number per image: the decoder maps one number z to one point of the plane, so all its outputs lie on one curve; the bends of the ReLU units let that curve bend.

title: Exercise: from PCA to autoencoders
text:
Where this leads
A plain autoencoder rebuilds its training images, but its latent space can have gaps: decode a point between training images and nothing guarantees a sensible image. The variational autoencoder (next unit) turns each image into a small cloud and keeps all clouds near one standard bell shape, so that the whole latent space decodes to plausible images and new images can be generated.

title: From PCA to autoencoders
text:
About this lecture
Can we describe an image with a few numbers, and rebuild it from them?

An image is a point in a space with one axis per pixel. Images of one kind fill only a thin part of it.
PCA finds the best flat summary: keep the score along a few directions.
PCA is an autoencoder: an encoder (image → few numbers) and a decoder (few numbers → image).
Replace both straight maps by neural networks: an autoencoder that can follow curved families of images.


This unit links PCA (eigenvectors of a covariance matrix) to neural networks (previous unit). If PCA was already covered in another unit (e.g. Shape models, where it gives the modes of variation of landmark shapes), the PCA slides are a recap; otherwise they are the introduction, from a two-pixel picture. The source of the “PCA is a linear autoencoder” example is the VAE unit of the 3MB00A course, there with two genes instead of two pixels.

title: From PCA to autoencoders
text:
An image is a point
A 28 \times 28 image is a vector of 784 grey values: one point in \mathbb R^{784}.

Almost every point of that space looks like noise. Handwritten digits, or masks of cells, fill a tiny, connected region of it.
Moving along that region changes the image smoothly: a little thicker, a little more tilted, a little longer.
So a few numbers should be enough to say where in the region an image is.

Today, start with images of two pixels: a point in the plane, which we can draw.

The two-pixel image is the whole unit in miniature: everything we do in the plane works in 784 dimensions, we just cannot draw it. Ask: if you change one pixel of a digit at random, is it still a digit? Almost always yes; if you change all pixels at random, almost never. The region of real images is thin.

title: From PCA to autoencoders
section: Neighbouring pixels: one number is almost enough
text:
Neighbouring pixels: one number is almost enough




Each dot: two neighbouring pixels of a smooth image. They are almost equally bright, so the dots lie along the diagonal.

Keep one number: the position along the blue line (the overall brightness).
Rebuild: go back to that point on the line.
Lost: the small difference between the pixels (red), the local edge.

The blue line is the direction of largest spread: the first principal component (PC1).


This is PCA for two pixels, from the picture. PC1 is (0.71, 0.70) for these data, essentially “both pixels together”, the average brightness; PC2 is “one minus the other”, a tiny edge. Natural images look like this: neighbouring pixels are strongly correlated, which is why images compress so well. The figure is the default state of the demo with the PCA button pressed.

title: From PCA to autoencoders
section: PCA is a linear autoencoder, by hand
text:
PCA is a linear autoencoder, by hand
Two pixels, mean subtracted. PC1 is the unit vector \mathbf u = (0.8,\ 0.6). Image \mathbf x = (3,\ 1).

Encode (image → one number): the score s = \mathbf u \cdot \mathbf x = 0.8 \cdot 3 + 0.6 \cdot 1 = 3.0.
Decode (number → image): \hat{\mathbf x} = s\,\mathbf u = 3.0 \cdot (0.8,\ 0.6) = (2.4,\ 1.8).
Error: \mathbf x - \hat{\mathbf x} = (0.6,\ -0.8), squared length 1.0.

With the mean added back: \text{encode}(\mathbf x) = \mathbf u^\top(\mathbf x - \bar{\mathbf x}), \ \text{decode}(s) = \bar{\mathbf x} + s\,\mathbf u.
With k components: k scores, and \hat{\mathbf x} = \bar{\mathbf x} + s_1\mathbf u_1 + \dots + s_k\mathbf u_k.

Encoder: project. Decoder: go back along the line. Every image on the PC1 line is rebuilt exactly; an image perpendicular to it has score 0 and is rebuilt as the mean image. In 784 dimensions, each u_k is itself an image (an “eigen-image”), and decoding adds eigen-images with the scores as weights.

title: From PCA to autoencoders
section: The math: why PCA is the best straight line
text:
The math: why PCA is the best straight line
Math layer: skip if you only want the idea.
Data \mathbf x_1, \dots, \mathbf x_n with mean \bar{\mathbf x} and covariance S = \frac1n\sum_i (\mathbf x_i - \bar{\mathbf x})(\mathbf x_i - \bar{\mathbf x})^\top. For a unit vector \mathbf u, with \mathbf y_i = \mathbf x_i - \bar{\mathbf x} (Pythagoras: \|\mathbf y\|^2 = (\mathbf u^\top\mathbf y)^2 + \|\mathbf y - (\mathbf u^\top\mathbf y)\mathbf u\|^2):
\frac1n\sum_i \big\|\mathbf y_i - (\mathbf u^\top\mathbf y_i)\,\mathbf u\big\|^2 = \underbrace{\frac1n\sum_i\|\mathbf y_i\|^2}_{\operatorname{tr} S} - \mathbf u^\top S\,\mathbf u.

Smallest error ⇔ largest \mathbf u^\top S\mathbf u ⇔ \mathbf u = the eigenvector of S with the largest eigenvalue \lambda_1. The error is then \operatorname{tr}S - \lambda_1 = \lambda_2 + \dots
With k components: the error is the sum of the dropped eigenvalues.
More generally (Baldi & Hornik 1989): any linear encoder and decoder with k numbers, trained on squared error, can do no better than PCA, and the best ones span the same subspace.


For the neighbouring-pixel data in the demo: S = [[0.0406, 0.0352], [0.0352, 0.0414]], eigenvalues 0.0762 and 0.0058, so the best one-number error is 0.0058 and keeping nothing (decode everything as the mean) costs tr S = 0.0820. At angle 0° (keep pixel 1 only) the error is tr S − S11 = 0.0820 − 0.0406 = 0.0414. The demo’s error-vs-angle plot is exactly tr S − uᵀSu.

title: From PCA to autoencoders
text:
The bottleneck must be narrow


Encoder: image → a few numbers z. Decoder: z → image. Train both so that \hat{\mathbf x} \approx \mathbf x for many images.
With as many numbers as pixels, the “autoencoder” just copies (PCA with all components: rotate, rotate back). It learns nothing.
A narrow bottleneck forces z to keep what varies most between images.


The digit is a real MNIST test image (a 7) encoded and decoded by the network of the last unit; the reconstruction is blurrier than the input because two numbers cannot hold every detail of the stroke. MNIST: Y. LeCun, C. Cortes, C. J. C. Burges; CC BY-SA 3.0 as stated in the Keras documentation.

title: From PCA to autoencoders
section: When the images lie on a curve
text:
When the images lie on a curve




A bright spot moves past two pixels. One true number (its position), but the images lie on a curve.

PC1 is the best straight line, yet the spot at position -0.5 and the spot at 0.2 (noise-free scores 0.42 and 0.46) get almost the same score: the line folds the curve.
PCA needs two numbers to rebuild these images well.



The spot is a Gaussian (sd 0.5 pixel) at positions from −0.5 to 1.5, seen by pixels at 0 and 1; noise-free pixel values at position −0.5 are (0.607, 0.011), at 0.2 they are (0.923, 0.278). The PC1 score is about (p1 − p2)/√2 up to the mean, which rises from 0.42 at −0.5 to 0.61 at 0 and falls back through 0.46 at 0.2. Starting far left, pixel 1 rises then falls while pixel 2 rises: the dots run along a horseshoe. Mean squared error with PC1: 0.0170, against 0.2642 for keeping nothing. A trajectory in any image family (a cell elongating, a digit getting thicker) behaves like this: it is curved in pixel space.

title: From PCA to autoencoders
text:
An autoencoder follows the curve




Replace both straight maps by small neural networks (unit Neural networks):
\text{encoder: } 2 \to 16 \to 1, \qquad \text{decoder: } 1 \to 16 \to 2 \quad (\text{ReLU}).

Still one number per image, but the decoder draws a curve (green) instead of a line.
Error after 1500 training steps: 0.0006, against 0.0170 for PCA.
Without the bends, this network would be a linear autoencoder: PCA again.



Same data, same one-number bottleneck. The decoder curve is the set of all images the decoder can produce: a one-dimensional family, bent to follow the data. Training is the downhill walk of the previous unit on the reconstruction error. Fixed seed; the demo reproduces exactly this curve.

title: From PCA to autoencoders
text:
From autoencoders to generating images
An autoencoder gives every image a place z in a small latent space, and a decoder that turns any z into an image.

Could we pick a new z and decode it, to make a new image?
A plain autoencoder only learns to rebuild its training images. Nothing says what lies between them in z, or where in z the images are.
The variational autoencoder (next unit) fixes this.

Idea
In one line

one axis per pixel; images of one kind fill a thin region

image → few numbers z → image

the best linear autoencoder: encode = project, decode = mean + scores × eigen-images


Error of PCA
the variance in the dropped directions (sum of dropped eigenvalues)


Bottleneck
must be narrow, or the network just copies


Autoencoder

title: Images in frequency space
text:
About this lecture

Every signal, and every image, is a sum of waves.
The discrete Fourier transform (DFT) is a change of basis to those waves.
In 2D, each coefficient is a plane wave with a direction and a frequency.
Convolution theorem: filtering = multiplying the spectrum. Low-pass, high-pass, notch.
Sampling: what a pixel grid can and cannot represent (aliasing).

title: Images in frequency space
section: Everything is a sum of waves
text:
Everything is a sum of waves
A signal on 0 \le t < 1 can be written as
f(t) = \sum_{k} c_k\, e^{2\pi i k t}, \qquad c_k = \int_0^1 f(t)\, e^{-2\pi i k t}\, dt.

Slow waves (small |k|) carry the broad shape; fast waves carry sharp edges and fine detail.
The coefficients come from an integral against each wave: a projection, because the waves are orthogonal.

title: Images in frequency space
text:
Try it: build a wave




Five waves sin(2π·f·t), f = 1 to 5 cycles per window; each slider sets one amplitude. The bold black line is the sum; the bars are the amplitude spectrum |a_f|. Start from a single slow wave, then add f = 3 at a third of the height and f = 5 at a fifth (or press “square”): plateaus with steep edges appear. Sharper edges would need still higher frequencies. “Sawtooth” uses all five with alternating signs. Point out that a negative amplitude flips the wave, a phase change, and the bars do not change: the amplitude spectrum throws away phase.

title: Images in frequency space
section: The DFT is a change of basis
text:
The DFT is a change of basis
For a signal of length N, x = (x_0, \dots, x_{N-1}):
X_k = \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} x_n\, e^{-2\pi i kn/N}, \qquad x_n = \frac1N \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} X_k\, e^{2\pi i kn/N}.

In matrix form, X = Fx with F_{kn} = e^{-2\pi i kn/N}. The columns of F^* are orthogonal: F^*F = N\,I.
So x and X are the same vector in two bases. Nothing is lost; F^{-1} = \tfrac1N F^*.
Parseval: \sum |x_n|^2 = \tfrac1N \sum |X_k|^2. Energy is shared out over the frequencies.
For real x: X_{N-k} = \overline{X_k}. Frequencies come in mirror pairs \pm k.
The FFT computes X in \mathcal{O}(N\log N) instead of \mathcal{O}(N^2).


This is the slide that should click for students with a linear algebra background: the Fourier transform is just an orthogonal (unitary, up to scale) change of basis. Index k = N − k is the same as frequency −k, which is why spectra are usually drawn with frequency 0 in the middle.

title: Images in frequency space
text:
From 1D to 2D: plane waves
For an N\times N image, the basis functions are
e^{2\pi i (ux + vy)/N}: \text{ a wave along the direction } (u, v), \text{ with } \sqrt{u^2+v^2} \text{ cycles across the image.}

The 2D DFT is the 1D DFT on every row, then on every column (it is separable).
We show the spectrum as \log(1 + |X_{u,v}|) with frequency (0, 0) in the centre.
Distance from the centre = frequency (fine vs coarse). Angle = orientation of the wave.
A pattern of stripes gives a pair of bright dots, perpendicular to the stripes.

title: Images in frequency space
text:
The convolution theorem
\mathcal{F}\{I * w\} = \mathcal{F}\{I\} \cdot \mathcal{F}\{w\}.
Convolution in the image = pointwise multiplication of the spectra. So every filter from last lecture has a frequency response \hat w(u, v):

Gaussian blur: \hat w is (close to) a Gaussian too, largest at 0: a low-pass filter.
Laplacian: \hat w \propto -(u^2 + v^2) near 0, zero at frequency 0: a high-pass filter.
Sum of weights = \hat w(0, 0): the response to the average brightness.

Large kernels are cheaper in frequency space: two FFTs and a product, \mathcal{O}(N^2\log N) for an N\times N image.

The FFT assumes the image repeats periodically, so filtering via FFT wraps around at the border: the “wrap” border rule from last time. Padding avoids it.

title: Images in frequency space
section: Try it: filter an image in frequency space
text:
Try it: filter an image in frequency space




Left: the image; middle: its spectrum (log magnitude, frequency 0 in the centre); right: the image rebuilt from the kept coefficients. Removed coefficients are dark red. Start with low-pass at max radius 30 and drag down to about 5: a blur, but the shape survives. Switch to high-pass: only edges and texture remain. Then “keep largest” at 3%: most of the variation is in very few coefficients, which is why JPEG works. Finally tick “add stripe artefact”, choose “no filter”, and erase the two bright dots (yellow rings): the stripe disappears. That is a notch filter.

title: Images in frequency space
text:
Sampling and aliasing
A pixel grid with spacing \Delta can only represent frequencies up to the Nyquist frequency \tfrac{1}{2\Delta}: two samples per cycle.

Finer detail is not lost silently: it folds back and appears as a false, coarser pattern (aliasing, moiré).
So before downsampling an image, blur it first (low-pass), to remove what the coarser grid cannot hold.
Same reason the optics of a microscope should match the pixel size of its camera.

title: Images in frequency space
text:
Summary

The DFT is an orthogonal change of basis to waves; nothing is lost.
Low frequencies = broad shapes; high frequencies = edges, texture and noise.
Convolution theorem: filtering is multiplication in frequency space. Kernels have a frequency response.
Isolated peaks in the spectrum = periodic structure (or artefacts): remove them with a notch.
Sample at least twice per cycle, and low-pass before downsampling.

title: Exercise: graph-cut segmentation
text:
Background







Idea
What it means




Nodes
one per pixel, plus s (object) and t (background)


t-links
s \to p with capacity D_p(0), p \to t with capacity D_p(1)


n-links
p \to q and q \to p, each with capacity \lambda w_{pq}, for 4-neighbours p, q


Labelling from a cut
L_p = 1 (object) if p is on the source side, else 0


Cut = energy
c(S, T) = \sum_p D_p(L_p) + \lambda \sum w_{pq}[L_p \ne L_q] = E(L)


Contrast weights
w_{pq} = \exp\!\big(-(I_p - I_q)^2/2\sigma^2\big); \sigma = \infty means w_{pq} = 1


Seeds
an object seed gets s \to p with infinite capacity; a background seed p \to t



Throughout, grey levels are 0 to 3 with \mu_0 = 0, \mu_1 = 3 and D_p(\ell) = (I_p - \mu_\ell)^2, so D_p(0) = I_p^2 and D_p(1) = (3 - I_p)^2. This is what the first demo uses.

title: Exercise: graph-cut segmentation
text:
By hand
B1. The 1 \times 3 image I = (3, 1, 3), with w_{pq} = 1. (a) Draw the graph: 5 nodes, 6 t-links, 2 pairs of n-links. Write every capacity for \lambda = 1. (b) List all 8 cuts (labellings) with their cost. Which is the minimum? Which labelling does thresholding give? (c) Repeat (b) for \lambda = 2. At which \lambda does the minimum change?
B2. Same image, now with contrast weights, \sigma = 1. (a) Compute w_{12} and w_{23}. What is w_{pq} for a grey-level difference of 1, and of 3? (b) Compute the energy of 101 and 111 for \lambda = 2 and \lambda = 5. Up to which \lambda does the dark pixel stay background? (c) Is that what you want if the dark pixel is noise? If it is a real gap between two objects?
B3. The 2 \times 2 image \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, 4-neighbours (4 pairs of n-links), w_{pq} = 1, \lambda = 2. Write labellings as top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right, e.g. 1100 = top row object. (a) Give the t-link capacities of the four pixels. (b) Compute the cost of the cuts 1100, 1000, 1110, 1111 and 0000. Then argue (or check by listing all 16) which cut is the minimum.
B4. Same 2 \times 2 image and \lambda, but the bottom-left pixel (grey level 1) is an object seed. Which capacities change? What is the minimum cut now, and its cost (counting the seed’s data cost D(1) = 4)?
B5. Shrinking bias. A 6 \times 6 image is 0 everywhere except column 2, which is a vertical line of grey level 2, and columns 4–6, a band of grey level 2 that touches the right border. Use w_{pq} = 1. (a) How much data cost does the line save by being object rather than background? How many n-links does labelling it object cut? Above which \lambda does the minimum drop the line? (b) The same for the band. (Its right side lies on the image border: no n-links there.) (c) Generalise: a long strip of width k pixels and data gain g per pixel. Above which \lambda is it removed?
B6. Metrication. Consider a long straight boundary in a large image with w_{pq} = 1. (a) With 4-neighbours, how many n-links does a horizontal boundary of length \ell cut? And a 45° staircase boundary of the same Euclidean length? (b) With 8-neighbours, horizontal and vertical n-links get weight \tfrac12, diagonal ones \tfrac{1}{2\sqrt2}. Compute the cost per unit length of a horizontal and of a 45° boundary. (c) Which neighbourhood gives the more “round” results, and why?

At \lambda = 1 the minimum is 101 (cost 3), the same as thresholding. (c) At \lambda = 2 the minimum is 111 (cost 4). 101 costs 1 + 2\lambda, 111 costs 4: they tie at \lambda = 1.5.
B2. (a) w_{12} = w_{23} = e^{-2^2/2} = e^{-2} = 0.135. For a difference of 1: e^{-0.5} = 0.607; of 3: e^{-4.5} = 0.011. (b) E(101) = 1 + \lambda \cdot 2 \cdot 0.135: 1.541 at \lambda = 2, 2.353 at \lambda = 5. E(111) = 4. The dark pixel stays background as long as 1 + 0.271\lambda < 4, i.e. up to \lambda = 11.08. (c) Contrast weights make a boundary across a large intensity jump almost free. That protects a real gap between two objects, but it also protects a noise pixel that differs strongly from its neighbours. \sigma should be larger than typical noise differences and smaller than the jumps at real edges.
B3. (a) Grey levels 3, 2, 1, 0: s \to p: 9, 4, 1, 0; p \to t: 0, 1, 4, 9. (b) 1100: data 0 + 1 + 1 + 0 = 2, n-links cut: top-left–bottom-left and top-right–bottom-right, 2, cost 2 + 2 \cdot 2 = 6. 1000: data 0 + 4 + 1 + 0 = 5, 2 n-links, cost 9. 1110: data 0 + 1 + 4 + 0 = 5, 2 n-links, cost 9. 1111: data 0 + 1 + 4 + 9 = 14, cost 14. 0000: data 9 + 4 + 1 + 0 = 14, cost 14. The minimum is 1100 with cost 6: it has the smallest possible data cost (each pixel takes its cheaper label, total 2), and any labelling with both labels cuts at least 2 n-links, so no labelling with a boundary can beat 2 + 4 = 6; the two without a boundary cost 14. Listing all 16 confirms it; the next best are 1000 and 1110 (9).
B4. The seed’s t-links become s \to p: \infty, p \to t: 0 (and its data cost D(1) = 4 is paid in any allowed labelling). Only labellings with bottom-left = 1 are allowed.
